list.listitem: Tourette syndrome (TS) is a hereditary neurological disorder characterized by multiple motor and 1 or more phonic tics, usually beginning in childhood. C

Diagnosis is clinical, relying on the identification of tics, and differentiating them from other movements or behaviors. Positive family history, and concurrent obsessive-compulsive or attention-deficit hyperactivity symptoms, support the diagnosis. C

Symptomatic drug therapy may be appropriate when tics affect function or quality of life. Neuroleptics have the most demonstrated efficacy, especially in severe cases, but for nondisabling tics the risk of long-term tardive movement disorder may outweigh their benefits. Alpha-agonists are a good initial option in mild to moderate cases. B

Tics in TS usually begin before puberty and may worsen for months to years. However, in late adolescence they usually improve significantly, sometimes resolving completely. Symptoms persist well into adulthood in a small fraction of cases. B

background.definition: Tourette syndrome is a neurological disorder characterized by multiple motor and 1 or more phonic tics, usually beginning in childhood. It lies on a neuropsychiatric spectrum that also includes obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and poor impulse control.

list.listitem: Prevalence estimates vary widely based on how inclusively TS is defined and based on the study population. Some studies suggest a lifetime prevalence for TS of 1 in 100.
There is thought to be a 3:1 male:female preponderance for TS. However, if OCD is included in the spectrum, the ratio is nearly equal.
TS is thought to be genetic, but the genes involved in most cases are not yet known.
Environmental factors, such as stress, may potentiate expression of the trait.
The evidence supporting immunological factors, such as exposure to group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, is controversial.
Pathogenesis is still unclear.
TS is thought to result from developmental abnormalities involving basal ganglia circuitry, especially inhibitory networks.
There is evidence for anomalous dopaminergic innervation and sensitivity within the striatum (part of the basal ganglia).
Although evidence for subtle neuroanatomic and neurochemical abnormalities is accumulating, TS is notable for the absence of gross pathological and radiological brain abnormalities.
TS is a hereditary neurological disorder characterized by multiple motor and 1 or more phonic tics, usually beginning in childhood. C

TS is a clinical diagnosis. The clinician must recognize tics (recurrent, brief, intermittent, stereotyped, nonrhythmic movements or sounds; often preceded by a sensation or urge and followed by a sense of relief; fluctuating over time). Tics must be differentiated from other movements or behaviors. C
The diagnosis is supported by a personal history of obsessive-compulsive or attention-deficit hyperactivity symptoms and a family history of such behavioral symptoms or tics. B
Consider secondary causes if you find neurological or developmental anomalies, onset in adulthood, or history of exposure to toxins or stimulants. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Follow a thought pattern or obsession, often ritualistic; respond to SSRI
Occur in organic brain disease, developmental delay, congenital blindness, etc
Controversial; sudden onset and remission after infections, history of chorea
Simple jerk of muscles, lack of premonitory sensation, often less suppressible
Onset usually in older adults, lack of other tic-like events or premonitory sensation
Progressive neurological decline, other accompanying features
Following exposure to stimulants, neuroleptics, some anticonvulsants

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: DSM-IV-TR criteria for Tourette syndrome are shown below: (1) Multiple motor and at least one vocal tic have been present at some time during the condition, not necessarily concurrently. (A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, nonrhythmic, stereotyped motor movement, or vocalization.) (2) Tics occur many times per day (usually in bouts), nearly every day or intermittently, through at least 1 year. During this period, there was never a tic-free period of more than 3 consecutive months. (3) Onset before age 18 years. (4) The disturbance is not due to the direct physiological effects of a substance (eg, stimulants) or a general medical condition (eg, Huntington's disease or postviral encephalitis). Note: because of the tremendous variability in primary tic disorders, and their increasingly recognized common neurobiological substrate, restrictive criteria for Tourette syndrome may not be clinically relevant. For example, a child with chronic motor tics who does not meet formal criteria for TS may still warrant similar treatment.

list.listitem: Tics are recurrent, brief, intermittent, stereotyped, nonrhythmic movements or sounds. Tics are usually preceded by a sensory premonition or urge and may be followed by a sense of relief. Tics often can be suppressed for a short time; alternatively, they may occur in repetitive bursts for a short time.
Examples of simple tics (more common): blinks, eye rolls, head tosses, grimaces, limb, or shoulder movements, sniffs, throat clearing, grunts.
Examples of complex tics (less common): touching, hitting, jumping, gesturing, utterances, profanities, verbal repetition.

Onset is overwhelmingly in childhood and adolescence, usually with improvement toward adulthood. Acquired tics of onset later in adulthood are unusual; consider secondary causes and specialist consultation.
Tics wax and wane in frequency and intensity; often worse with stress. In the long term, certain tics may disappear while others appear.
For some patients, tics may be very bothersome or interfere with life activities. Others are not bothered by them, although friends and family might notice them.
They are commonly associated with obsessive-compulsive symptoms, ADHD, and anxiety. Self-injurious behaviors and conduct disorders may be present.
A family history of tics or related behavioral disorders supports the diagnosis.
Tics may be seen on examination. Neurological examination should otherwise be unremarkable.
There are currently no diagnostic tests to identify TS or monitor its course.

Imaging or other studies are not routinely recommended. Consider further testing if a secondary cause is suspected (neurological or developmental anomalies, onset in adulthood, or history of exposure to toxins or stimulants).
TS is a clinical diagnosis. No laboratory tests (including imaging or biomarkers) can currently establish the diagnosis.
The diagnosis is supported by a personal or family history of impulse control problems, ADHD, or OCD or a family history of tics.

The history and physical should exclude secondary causes of tics or stereotypies. In suspicious cases, laboratory tests may help to identify secondary causes of tic-like behaviors (including stimulant abuse, Huntington disease, or other organic brain disease).
If concurrent OCD, ADHD, or anxiety symptoms are more severe than tics, prioritize treatment of these first. C
Available treatment is only symptomatic. Mild tics may require no treatment. C
Alpha-agonists (clonidine or guanfacine) are often used first line for mild to moderate, nondisabling tics that affect functioning and quality of life. B

Neuroleptics (notably pimozide, haloperidol, or risperidone) are are consistently effective but are best reserved for severe or disabling tics, given the small but real risk of long-term tardive movement disorder. A

Existing therapy is symptomatic. There is no evidence that it modifies or prevents the condition, and mild cases are often managed without medication. If non-tic symptoms predominate (eg, OCD and ADHD symptoms), treat those first.

Medication is appropriate if tics affect school or job performance, social interaction, or activities of daily living. Start medication at a low dose and titrate gradually to the lowest dose that tolerably suppresses tics.
Since the condition fluctuates naturally, it takes time to determine treatment success or failure. Attempt slowly to taper medications during periods of sustained improvement or low stress.

Alpha-agonists are often used first line for mild to moderate tics. Clonidine has more evidence supporting its efficacy than guanfacine, but the latter is less sedating. They may also help suppress oppositional and hyperactive behavior as seen in ADHD.

Dopamine receptor blockers (neuroleptics) have the most evidence for suppressing tics. Pimozide and haloperidol are FDA approved for TS and showed success in higher quality trials. Risperidone has also shown efficacy. Other neuroleptics may work but have less data.

Neuroleptic therapy may cause a long-term tardive movement disorder, beside shorter term side effects, including prolonged QT, sedation, and weight gain. Many specialists therefore reserve neuroleptics for treatment of severe or disabling tics.
Many other agents have shown success in small pilot trials and specialist experience. These include clonazepam and the anticonvulsants topiramate and levetiracetam.
Tetrabenazine, a dopamine depleter, has demonstrated promise.
SSRIs are indicated for significant obsessive-compulsive or anxiety components but have not been shown to ameliorate tics.

The medical cannabinoid dronabinol is associated with a large benefit in patients with Tourette syndrome (a standardized mean difference on symptom scores of 1.01 SD lower). However adverse events were more common with all cannabinoids (147 to 251 more events per 1000 persons treated).
A systematic review of 5 RCTs found no evidence to support the efficacy of vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 (VMAT2) inhibitors for treatment of tic disorders including TS.
A randomized trial found no benefit of ondansetron.
Anecdotally, deep brain stimulation has helped in a few refractory severe cases. Further studies are needed.
A meta-analysis of transcranial magnetic stimulation found 4 RCTs with only 72 patients. No effect on tic severity was observed.
Cannabis therapy was effective based on a meta-analysis of 3 studies with 401 adult patients.
A systematic review found that acupuncture if effective, but the quality of included studies was very limited.

"Habit Reversal Training" (including "awareness training with self-monitoring" "relaxation train" and competing response training") has shown efficacy in several studies, including controlled trials. Its practical value is still being established.
Psychotherapy may help some patients cope better with stress, with fewer tics as a result. Evidence for this is lacking.
Comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics (CBIT) effectively reduced tic severity in patients with Tourett syndrome.
Online, remotely delivered exposure and response prevention therapy is effective for tic disorder, based on a RCT with 224 participants.
Rarely, severe tics may result in self-injury, which must be appropriately managed.

Tics in TS usually begin between the ages of 3 and 15 years, most commonly at about age 7. Most patients experience significant improvement, often with complete resolution, beginning in late adolescence. B
Symptoms persist well into adulthood in a small fraction of cases. C
There are currently no genetic or biological markers that can predict the course in a given patient. C
TS is hereditary; TS brains are "wired differently" in a way that causes tics.
Tics vary in severity and usually improve after childhood.
Tics do not always need treatment. Parents should not seek treatment for a child who is otherwise functioning well socially, academically, and physically.
In fact, many successful individuals, in all walks of life, have TS.
